learningObjective: Explain the difference between saturation and wrap-around handling of out-of-range values in integer quantization.
stem: During INT8 quantization, a value exceeds the representable range (e.g., quantize(x/s) = 200 > 127). Which is the correct comparison of saturation vs. wrap-around handling?

options.text: Saturation and wrap-around are equivalent modulo a sign flip; both preserve the underlying signal.

Saturation clamps the out-of-range value to the boundary (200 → 127); this loses information about the extreme but preserves ordinal relationships and is the mathematically-desired behavior for neural-network quantization. Wrap-around uses modular arithmetic (200 → 200-256 = -56); it turns a large positive into a moderately-negative value, which is catastrophic for signal-carrying activations.
Wrap-around is the mathematically-desired behavior because it preserves the exact bit-count of the value.
Saturation is only used for weights; activations always use wrap-around because it is what CUDA integer instructions default to.

explanation: Saturation clamps out-of-range results to the nearest representable extreme, preserving monotonicity of the mapping and avoiding catastrophic sign flips. Wrap-around (two's-complement modular arithmetic) is the default behavior of raw integer arithmetic on most hardware; if applied naively during quantization, it produces values that are semantically nonsensical (a large positive becomes a large negative). Quantization frameworks (TensorRT, PyTorch, ONNX Q/DQ, cuDNN) all use saturation. Options A, C, D are wrong: A wrongly equates saturation with wrap-around, C prefers wrap-around, and D artificially restricts saturation to weights only.

optionExplanations.B: Correct: saturation preserves ordinal semantics; wrap-around is catastrophic.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: bit-count preservation is irrelevant to signal preservation.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: saturation is used for both weights and activations.

assumptions: Standard integer quantization for DNN inference; not a bit-level cryptographic use case.
nonImplications: Does not imply saturation is free — repeated saturation on many activations indicates a scale choice problem.
Does not imply wrap-around is never used — some cryptographic or checksum contexts require it.
